# 1 Introduction and Overview

## 1.1 Basic Concepts

This vignette introduces the aifeducation package and its usage with *R* syntax. We recommend that users who are unfamiliar with *R* or who lack coding skills in relevant languages (e.g. Python) start with the graphical user interface *AI for Education - Studio* which
is described in the vignette [02 Using the graphical user interface
Aifeducation - Studio](gui_aife_studio.html).

We assume that *aifeducation* is installed as described in the vignette [01
Get
Started](https://fberding.github.io/aifeducation/articles/aifeducation.html).
The introduction begins with a brief explanation of the basic concepts necessary for working with this package.

In the social and educational sciences, it is important to attribute scientific concepts to observations. This enables researchers to comprehend the observation, generate new insights, and develop recommendations for research and practice.

In educational science, several areas deal with this kind of task. For example, diagnosing students' characteristics is an important part of a teacher's role and necessary for understanding and promoting learning.
Another example is learning analytics, which uses data about students to create learning environments adapted to their individual needs. Similarly, educational institutions such as schools and universities can use this information to make data-driven decisions about performance (Laurusson & White 2014), as well as identifying areas for improvement. In any case, real-world observations are aligned with scientific models in order to apply scientific knowledge as a technology to improve learning and instruction.

Supervised machine learning is a concept that establishes a link between real-world observations and existing scientific models and theories (Berding et al. 2022). For educational science, this is advantageous because it enables researchers to apply AI using existing knowledge and insights. However, this approach has a drawback: training AI requires information about real-world observations and the corresponding alignment with scientific models and theories.

Written texts are a valuable source of data in educational science, since textual data can be found almost everywhere in the realm of learning and teaching (Berding et al. 2022). For example, teachers often set tasks for students to complete in written form.
Students then have to create a solution to the task, which they often document with a short written essay or presentation. This data can be used to analyse learning and teaching. Teachers' written tasks may provide insights into the quality of instruction, while students' solutions may provide insights into their learning outcomes and prerequisites.

AI can be a helpful assistant when it comes to analysing textual data, since this is a challenging and time-consuming task for humans.

>Please note that this vignette does not cover an introduction to content analysis, natural language processing or machine learning.
>If you would like to learn more, please refer to the cited literature.

Before we begin, we must introduce our definitions of some basic concepts, since applying AI to educational contexts involves combining knowledge from different scientific disciplines that use different — and sometimes overlapping — concepts. Even within a single research area, concepts are not unified.
Figure `r running_num_figures` illustrates the approach adopted in this package.

![Figure `r running_num_figures`: Understanding of Central Concepts](classif_fig_01.png){width="100%"}
```{r, include = FALSE}
running_num_figures <- running_num_figures + 1
```

Since *aifeducation* looks at the application of AI for classification tasks from the perspective of the empirical method of content analysis, there is some overlap between the concepts of content analysis and machine learning. In content analysis, phenomena such as performance or colours can be described as a scale or dimension made up of several categories (e.g. Schreier 2012, pp. 59). In our example, an exam performance could be described as "good", "average" or "poor". In terms of colours, categories could be "blue", "green", etc. The machine learning literature uses different terminology to describe this type of data. In machine learning, 'scale' and 'dimension' correspond to the term 'label', while 'categories' correspond to the term 'classes' (Chollet, Kalinowski & Allaire 2022, p. 114).

With these clarifications, classification means assigning a text to the correct category on a scale, or labelling the text with the correct class. As illustrated in Figure `r running_num_figures`, two types of data are required to train an AI to classify text in accordance with supervised machine learning principles.

![Figure `r running_num_figures`: Basic Structure of Supervised Machine Learning](classif_fig_02.png){width="100%"}

```{r, include = FALSE}
running_num_figures <- running_num_figures + 1
```

By providing AI with textual data as input and class-specific target data, it can learn to recognise texts that imply a specific class or category. In the above exam example, the AI can learn to recognise texts that imply a "good", "average" or "poor" judgement. Once trained, the AI can be applied to new texts to predict their class. This classification can then be used for further statistical analysis or to derive recommendations about learning and teaching.

In use cases as described in this vignette, AI has to "understand" natural language:
„Natural language processing is an area of research in
computer science and artificial intelligence (AI) concerned with
processing natural languages such as English and Mandarin. This
processing generally involves translating natural language into data
(numbers) that a computer can use to learn about the world. (…)” (Lane ,
Howard & Hapke 2019, p. 4)

Thus, the first step is to transform raw text into a form usable by a computer. This involves converting raw text into numbers.
In modern approaches, this is typically achieved using word embeddings.
Campesato (2021, p. 102) describes these as "the collective name for a
set of language modeling and feature learning techniques (...) where
words or phrases from the vocabulary are mapped to vectors of real
numbers." The definition of a word vector is similar: „Word vectors
rePostsent the semantic meaning of words as vectors in the context of the
training corpus." (Lane, Howard & Hapke 2019, p. 191). In the next step, the words or text embeddings can be used as the input data and the labels as the target data when training an AI system to classify text.

In *aifeducation,* these steps are covered with three different types of
models, as shown in Figure `r running_num_figures`.

![Figure `r running_num_figures`: Model Types in aifeducation](classif_model_hierachy.png){width="100%"}

```{r, include = FALSE}
running_num_figures <- running_num_figures + 1
```

-   **Base Models:** The base models have the ability to understand natural language. 
    These are generally transformers such as BERT and RoBERTa. A large number of 
    pre-trained models can be found on  [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/).

-   **Text Embedding Models:** These models are built on top of base models and 
    store instructions for using these base models to convert raw text into sequences 
    of numbers. Please note that the same base model can be used to create different text embedding models.

-   **Classifiers:** Classifiers are used in conjunction with a text embedding model. 
    They classify text into categories or classes based on the numeric representation 
    provided by the corresponding text embedding model. Please note that a text embedding 
    model can be used to create different classifiers (e.g. one for colours, one to estimate text quality, etc.).

# 2 Start Working

## 2.1 Starting a New Session

Before you can start working with *aifeducation*, you must set up a new R session. First, load aifeducation.
Next, you need to set up Python via 'reticulate' and select the environment in which all the necessary Python libraries are available.  If you installed Python as suggested in vignette [01 Get started](aifeducation.html), you can start a new session like this:

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
library(aifeducation)
prepare_session()
```

>Please remember: Each time you start a new session in *R*, you must load the *aifeducation* library and configure Python. 
>We recommend using the function 'prepare_session' because it performs all the necessary steps for correctly setting up Python.

Now you can start your work.

## 2.2 Data Management

### 2.2.1 Introduction

In the context of use cases for *aifeducation,* three different types of
data are necessary: raw text, text embeddings and target data, which 
represent the categories/classes of a text.

To address the first two types and enable the use of large data sets that may exceed your machine's memory capacity, the package ships with two specialised objects.

The first is `LargeDataSetForText`. Objects of this class are used to read raw text from .txt, .pdf and .xlsx files and store it for further computations. The second is the `LargeDataSetForTextEmbeddings` class, which stores the text embeddings of raw texts generated with `TextEmbeddingModel`s. We will describe the transformation of raw texts into text embeddings later.

### 2.2.2 Raw Texts

You need to create a `LargeDataSetForText` if you want to create or train a base model or generate text embeddings. If you are creating such a dataset for the first time, you must first create an empty dataset.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = FALSE}
raw_texts <- LargeDataSetForText$new()
```

Different methods are available to fill this object with raw texts, depending on the file type used for storing them.

**.txt files**

The first alternative is to store raw texts in .txt files. To use these
you have to structure your data in a specific way:

-   Create a main folder for storing your data.
-   Store every raw text/document into a *single* .txt file into its
    *own* folder within the main folder. In every folder there should be
    only one file for a raw text/document.
-   Add an additional .txt file to the folder named `bib_entry.txt`.
    This file contains bibliographic information for the raw text.
-   Add an additional .txt file to the folder named `license.txt` which
    contains a short statement for the license of the text such as "CC
    BY".
-   Add an additional .txt file to the folder named `url_license.txt`
    which contains the url/link to the license's text such as
    "<https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/>".
-   Add an additional .txt file to the folder named `text_license.txt`
    which contains the full license in raw texts.
-   Add an additional .txt file to the folder named `url_source.txt`
    which contains the url/link to the text file in the internet.

Applying these rules may result in a data structure as follows:

-   Folder "main folder"
    -   Folder Text A
        -   text_a.txt
        -   bib_entry.txt
        -   license.txt
        -   url_license.txt
        -   text_license.txt
        -   url_source.txt
    -   Folder Text B
        -   text_b.txt
        -   bib_entry.txt
        -   license.txt
        -   url_license.txt
        -   text_license.txt
        -   url_source.txt
    -   Folder Text C
        -   text_C.txt
        -   bib_entry.txt
        -   license.txt
        -   url_license.txt
        -   text_license.txt
        -   url_source.txt

Now you can call the method `add_from_files_txt` by passing the path to
the directory of the main folder to `dir_path`.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = FALSE}
raw_texts$add_from_files_txt(
  dir_path = "main folder",
  clean_text = TRUE
)
```

The data set will now read all the raw texts in the main folder and assign each text the corresponding bibliographic entry, licence, etc. Please note that adding a bib_entry.txt, license.txt, url_license.txt, text_license.txt and url_source.txt to every folder is optional.
If there is no such file in the corresponding folder, an empty entry will appear in the dataset. However, against the backdrop of the European AI Act, we recommend providing both the licence and bibliographic information to make documenting your models more straightforward. Furthermore, some licences, such as those provided by Creative Commons, require statements about the creators, a copyright note, a URL or link to the source material (if possible), the licence of the material, and a URL or link to the licence text online, or the licence text itself. Please check the licences of the material you are using to determine the specific requirements.

**.pdf files**

The second alternative is to use .pdf files as a source for raw texts.
The necessary structure here is similar to that of .txt files:

-   Create a main folder for storing your data.
-   Store every raw text/document into a *single* .pdf file into its
    *own* folder within the main folder. In every folder there should be
    only one file for a raw text/document.
-   Add an additional .txt file to the folder named `bib_entry.txt`.
    This file contains bibliographic information for the raw text.
-   Add an additional .txt file to the folder named `license.txt` which
    contains a short statement for the license of the text such as "CC
    BY".
-   Add an additional .txt file to the folder named `url_license.txt`
    which contains the URL/link to the license's text such as
    "<https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/>".
-   Add an additional .txt file to the folder named `text_license.txt`
    which contains the full license in raw texts.
-   Add an additional .txt file to the folder named `url_source.txt`
    which contains the url/link to the text file in the internet.

Applying these rules may result in a data structure as follows:

-   Folder "main folder"
    -   Folder Text A
        -   text_a.pdf
        -   bib_entry.txt
        -   license.txt
        -   url_license.txt
        -   text_license.txt
        -   url_source.txt
    -   Folder Text B
        -   text_b.pdf
        -   bib_entry.txt
        -   license.txt
        -   url_license.txt
        -   text_license.txt
        -   url_source.txt
    -   Folder Text C
        -   text_C.pdf
        -   bib_entry.txt
        -   license.txt
        -   url_license.txt
        -   text_license.txt
        -   url_source.txt

>Please note that all files except the text file should have a .txt extension, not a .pdf extension.

Now you can call the method `add_from_files_pdf` by passing the path to
the directory of the main folder to `dir_path`.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = FALSE}
raw_texts$add_from_files_pdf(
  dir_path = "main folder",
  clean_text = TRUE
)
```

As stated above, `bib_entry.txt`, `license.txt`, `url_license.txt`, `text_license.txt` and `url_source.txt` are optional.

**.xlsx files**

The third option is to save the raw texts as .xlsx files. This alternative is useful if you have many small raw texts. For very large texts, such as books or papers, we recommend storing them as .txt or .pdf files.

In order to add raw text from .xlsx files, the files need a special structure:

-   Create a main folder for storing all the .xlsx files that you want to read.
-   All .xlsx files must contain the names of the columns in the first row, and these names 
    must be identical for each column across all the files you wish to read.
-   Each .xlsx file must contain a column for storing the text ID and a column 
    for storing the raw text. Every text must have a unique ID across all .xlsx files.
-   Each .xlsx file can contain an additional column for the bibliographic entry.
-   Every .xlsx file can contain an additional column for the licence.
-   Every .xlsx file can contain an additional column for the licence URL.
-   Every .xslx file can contain an additional column for the licence text.
-   Every .xlsx file can contain an additional column for the source's URL.

Your .xlsx file might look something like this:

| id | text | bib | license | url_license | text_license | url_source |
|-----------|-----------|-----------|-----------|-----------|-----------|-----------|
| z3 | This is an example. | Author (2019) | CC BY | Example URL | Text | Example URL |
| a3 | This is a second example. | Author (2022) | CC BY | Example URL | Text | Example URL |
| ... | ... | ... | ... |  |  |  |

You can now call the method `add_from_files_xlsx` by passing the path to the main folder directory to `dir_path`. Remember to specify the column names for ID and text, as well as for the other columns.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = FALSE}
raw_texts$add_from_files_xlsx(
  dir_path = "main folder",
  id_column = "id",
  text_column = "text",
  bib_entry_column = "bib_entry",
  license_column = "license",
  url_license_column = "url_license",
  text_license_column = "text_license",
  url_source_column = "url_source"
)
```


**Clean text**

For .txt and .pdf files, set the argument `clean_text=TRUE`. This will prompt an algorithm to post-process the raw text and apply the following modifications:
 
* Some special symbols are removed.
* All spaces at the beginning and end of a line are removed.
* Multiple spaces are reduced to a single space.
* All rows containing a number from 1 to 999 at the beginning or end (header and footer) are removed.
* The list of contents is removed.
* Hyphenation is undone.
* Line breaks within a paragraph are removed.
* Multiple line breaks are reduced to a single line break.

These changes aim to provide clean plain text to increase the performance and quality of all analyses.

**IDs**
For .xlsx files, the text IDs are set to the IDs stored in the corresponding ID column. For .pdf and .txt files, the file names are used as the ID (without the file extension).

> Please note that a consequence of this is that two files *text_01.txt*
> and *text_01.pdf* have the same ID, which is not allowed. Please
> ensure that you use unique IDs across file formats.

**Saving and loading a data set**

Once you have created a `LargeDataSetForText`, you can save your data to disk by calling the `save_to_disk` function. In our example, the code would be as follows:

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = FALSE}
save_to_disk(
  object = raw_texts,
  dir_path = "examples",
  folder_name = "raw_texts"
)
```

The argument `object` requires the object that you would like to save. In our case, this is 'raw_texts'. With `dir_path`, you specify the location in which to save the object, and with `folder_name`, you define the name of the folder that will be created within that directory. The data set is saved in this folder.

To load an existing data set, call the function `load_from_disk` with the directory path where you stored the data. In our case, this would be:

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = FALSE}
raw_text_dataset <- load_from_disk("examples/raw_texts")
```

Now you can work with your data.

### 2.2.3 Text Embeddings

The numerical representations of raw text, known as text embeddings, are stored with objects of the class `LargeDataSetForTextEmbeddings.` These kinds of data sets are generated by models such as `TextEmbeddingModel.` Therefore, it is not necessary to create such a data set manually.

However, you will need this type of data set to train a classifier or predict the categories/classes of raw texts. Therefore, it may be advantageous to save transformed data. You can save and load an object of this class using the functions `save_to_disk` and `load_from_disk`.

Let us assume that we have a `LargeDataSetForTextEmbeddings` called
*text_embeddings*. Saving this object might look like this:

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = FALSE}
save_to_disk(
  object = text_embeddings,
  dir_path = "examples",
  folder_name = "text_embeddings"
)
```

The dataset will be saved in the 'examples/text_embeddings' folder. Loading this data set may look like this:

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = FALSE}
new_text_embeddings <- load_from_disk("examples/text_embeddings")
```

### 2.2.4 Target Data

The final data type required for working with *aifeducation* is the categories/classes of the raw text provided. We currently do not provide a special object for this kind of data. You just need a *named* `factor` storing the classes/categories for a dimension. It is also important that the names equal the ID of the corresponding raw texts/text embeddings, as matching the classes/categories to texts is done using these names.

Saving and loading can be done with *R*'s functions `save` and `load`.

## 2.3 Example Data for this Vignette

To illustrate the steps in this vignette, we cannot use data from educational settings, as such data are generally protected by privacy policies. Therefore, we have used a subset of the Stanford Movie Review Dataset, which was provided by Maas et al. (2011) and is included in the package. You can access the dataset with `imdb_movie_reviews.`

We now have a dataset with three columns. The first contains the raw text, the second the rating of the film (positive or negative) and the third the ID of the film review. Approximately 200 reviews imply a positive rating of a film, and around 100 imply a negative rating.

In this tutorial, we will modify the data set by setting approximately 50 positive and 25 negative reviews to `NA`, to indicate that these reviews are unlabelled.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
example_data <- imdb_movie_reviews
example_data$label <- as.character(example_data$label)
example_data$label[c(76:100)] <- NA
example_data$label[c(201:250)] <- NA
table(example_data$label)
```
We will now create a `LargeDataSetForText` object from this `data.frame`.
Before we can do this, however, we must ensure that the data set has all the necessary columns.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
colnames(example_data)
```

Now, we need to add two columns. For this tutorial, we will not be adding any bibliographic or licence information, although this is recommended in practice.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
example_data$bib_entry <- NA
example_data$license <- NA
colnames(example_data)
```

The `data.frame` is now ready as input for our data set. The 'label' column will not be included.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
data_set_reviews_text <- LargeDataSetForText$new()
data_set_reviews_text$add_from_data.frame(example_data)
```

You can inspect the data set with `print`.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
print(data_set_reviews_text)
```

We save the categories/labels within a separate `factor`.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
review_labels <- as.factor(example_data$label)
names(review_labels) <- example_data$id
```

We will now use this data to demonstrate how to use the various objects and functions in *aifeducation*.

# 3 Base Models

## 3.1 Overview

Base models form the foundation of all subsequent models in *aifeducation*.
Currently, these are Transformer models such as ModernBERT (Warner et al. 2024), MPNet (Song et al. 2020), BERT (Devlin et al. 2019), RoBERTa (Liu et al. 2019) and Funnel-Transformer (Dai et al. 2020). In general, these models are first trained on a large corpus of general texts. Next, the models are fine-tuned to domain-specific texts and/or specific tasks. As creating base models requires a large amount of text, resulting in high computational time, it is recommended to use pre-trained models. These can be found on [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/). However, sometimes it is more straightforward to create a new model to fit a specific purpose. Sometimes, however, it is more
straightforward to create a new model to fit a specific purpose.
*aifeducation* supports the option to create and train/fine-tune base models.

In this chapter, we focus on developing a new model. Chapter 4 describes the use of a pre-trained model from [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/). Each transformer model comprises two parts: 

1.  The tokenizer, which splits raw text into smaller pieces in order to model a large number of 
    words using a limited number of tokens.
2.  The neural network, which is used to model the capability to understand natural language.

## 3.2 Creation of a Tokenizer

The first step is to set up a tokenizer. In *aifeducation*, you can choose from a variety of models. In this example, we use a `WordPieceTokenizer.` To create a new tokenizer, we first call the `new` method.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
tokenizer <- WordPieceTokenizer$new()
```

We now have an empty tokenizer that can be configured by calling the relevant method.
The available parameters depend on the type of tokenizer. In the case of a `WordPieceTokenizer`, we only have two options. The first, `vocab_size`, determines how many tokens the tokenizer should recognise. The second (`vocab_do_lower_case`) determines whether all words should be transformed to lowercase before tokenization. Since we are only using a very small data set to illustrate the usage of the package, we set `vocab_size = 200`. In real-world applications, this value should be larger.
You can find more information on this topic in the vignette [04 Model configuration and training](model_configuration.html).

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
tokenizer$configure(
  vocab_size = 200,
  vocab_do_lower_case = FALSE
)
```

The next step is to train the model by calling the `train` method. Here, we pass a text data set to the parameter `text_dataset`. This raw text is then used to train the model. 

In addition, we can use the Python library `codecarbon` to set up sustainability tracking of this process and estimate its ecological impact. Therefore, the `sustain_track` parameter is set to `TRUE` by default.
If you use the sustainability tracker, you must provide the three-letter code for the country in which your computer is located (e.g. "CAN" for Canada, "DEU" for Germany). You can find a list of these codes on
[Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_3166-1_alpha-3). This is because different countries use different sources and techniques for generating energy, resulting in a specific impact on CO₂ emissions. For the USA and Canada, you can also specify a region by setting sustain_region. Please refer to the 'codecarbon' documentation for more information.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
tokenizer$train(
  text_dataset = data_set_reviews_text,
  statistics_max_tokens_length = 512,
  sustain_track = TRUE,
  sustain_iso_code = "DEU",
  sustain_region = NULL,
  sustain_interval = 15,
  sustain_log_level = "error",
  trace = TRUE
)
```

Training a tokenizer is a very fast process. Therefore, even a large quantity of texts should only take a few minutes to process. The model is now ready to use. Initially, we can explore some tokeniser statistics.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
# We use t() to improve the readability of the table
t(tokenizer$get_tokenizer_statistics())
```

```{r, include = FALSE, eval = TRUE}
mu_g <- tokenizer$get_tokenizer_statistics()$mu_g
```

This table provides an estimation of the number of words in the entire training dataset, the total number of tokens resulting from the raw texts, and the number of sequences if the length of a sequence is limited to the value shown in the 'max_token_length' column.
Furthermore, the three statistics proposed by Kaya and Tantug (2024, p. 5) are shown.

- $\mu_t$ refers to the average number of tokens per sequence, 
- $\mu_w$ refers to the average number of words per sequence, and 
- $\mu_g$ refers to the average number of tokens per word.

The tokenizer granularity rate, $\mu_g$, describes how many tokens are necessary to represent a single word. This value is important because a higher value means that the same text is split into a longer sequence of tokens than with a tokenizer with a lower value. Since large language models have a maximum limit on the length of a token sequence, this value impacts how many words of a text can be processed by a base model.

To see how the tokenizer works, call the `encode` method.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
tokenizer$encode(
  raw_text = "This is a good movie.",
  token_encodings_only = TRUE,
  token_to_int = FALSE
)
```

As you can see here, the tokenizer splits the words into several tokens and adds some special tokens.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
tokenizer$encode(
  raw_text = "This is a good movie.",
  token_encodings_only = TRUE,
  token_to_int = TRUE
)
```

Changing the parameter to `token_to_int = TRUE` produces the same result, but instead of the tokens, you get the index of the token in the tokenizer's vocabulary.
For example, in this example, the ID 0 refers to the token [CLS].

If you have a sequence of IDs and would like to know which tokens correspond to these numbers, you can call the `decode` method.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
tokenizer$decode(
  int_seqence = list(list(c(0, 53, 109, 174, 188, 61, 67, 97, 97, 112, 73, 97, 110, 99, 101, 17, 1))),
  to_token = TRUE
)
```

If you would like to analyse the ecological impact of training the tokenizer, you can get an estimate of the energy consumption and CO₂ emissions involved.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
# We use t() to improve the readability of the table
t(tokenizer$get_sustainability_data("training"))
```

Since tokenizers can be trained very efficiently, these values will usually be very low.

Finally, you can save and load your model. This is done for all objects using the functions `save_to_disk` and `load_from_disk`.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
save_to_disk(
  object = tokenizer,
  dir_path = "examples",
  folder_name = "example_tokenizer"
)
```


```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
tokenizer <- load_from_disk("examples/example_tokenizer")
```

To get a short summary of a tokenizer you can use `print`.
```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
print(tokenizer)
```

Now you are ready to create a base model.

## 3.3 Creating a BaseModel

At the outset, you can select from the various supported transformer architectures. Depending on the architecture chosen, different options are available for determining the shape of your neural network. For this vignette, we use a BERT model (Devlin et al. 2019).

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
base_model_bert <- BaseModelBert$new()
base_model_bert$configure(
  tokenizer = tokenizer,
  max_position_embeddings = 512,
  hidden_size = 64,
  num_hidden_layers = 4,
  num_attention_heads = 4,
  intermediate_size = 2 * 64,
  hidden_act = "GELU",
  hidden_dropout_prob = 0.1,
  attention_probs_dropout_prob = 0.1
)
```

First, we create an empty model with 'new'. You can then configure your model in the next step.
The available parameters depend on the model type. In this example, we create a model with four hidden layers, a hidden size of 64 and four attention heads. The maximum sequence length is 512 tokens. 
Since the tokenizer granularity rate is `r mu_g` this
allows the model to process an average of `r mu_g*512` words.

Please note that the value of the `max_position_embeddings` parameter determines how many tokens your transformer can process. If your text contains more tokens than this number, the additional tokens are ignored. However, if you would like to analyse long documents, please avoid increasing this number too significantly because the computational time increases quadratically rather than linearly (Beltagy, Peters & Cohan 2020). For long documents, you can use another Transformer architecture (e.g. Longformer, Beltagy, Peters & Cohan 2020), or split a long document into several sequential chunks for classification (e.g. Pappagari et al. 2019). Using chunks is supported by *aifedcuation* for all models.

The parameter `tokenizer` requires a tokenizer object. Here, we use the model created in Section 3.2.

> The vignette [04 Model configuration and training](model_configuration.html)
> provides details on how to configure a base model.

Your model is now ready. You can either save it using the `save_to_disk` function or continue with training.

## 3.3 Train/Fine-Tune a Base Model

If you want to train a new base model for the first time (see section 3.2) or adapt a pre-trained model to a domain-specific language or task, you can call the corresponding `train` method.

```{r base_model_bert$train, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
base_model_bert$train(
  text_dataset = data_set_reviews_text,
  p_mask = 0.30,
  whole_word = TRUE,
  val_size = 0.1,
  n_epoch = 10,
  batch_size = 12,
  max_sequence_length = 250,
  full_sequences_only = FALSE,
  min_seq_len = 50,
  learning_rate = 3e-3,
  sustain_track = TRUE,
  sustain_iso_code = "DEU",
  sustain_region = NULL,
  sustain_interval = 15,
  sustain_log_level = "error",
  trace = TRUE,
  pytorch_trace = 0,
  log_dir = NULL,
  log_write_interval = 2
)
```

The data for training must be passed to `text_dataset`. This object should be of the `LargeDataSetForText` class, as described in Section 2.2.2.
In this example, we use text from movie reviews. Please note that this data set is too small for training a new Transformer. We are using it here only to provide a quick demonstration. 
For real use cases, a larger data set is necessary.

For a Bert model, the learning objective is masked language modelling. 
Other models may use different learning objectives. Please refer to the documentation for more details on each model.
You can set how masking is done using the `p_mask` and `whole_word` parameters. If `whole_word` is set to `FALSE`, a number of tokens are masked. If `whole_word` is set to `TRUE`, all tokens belonging to a specific number of words are masked. The number of words/tokens is chosen using `p_mask`.

You can set the length of token sequences using the `max_sequence_length` parameter, which instructs the tokenizer to split long texts into several sequences of the specified size. Using the `val_size` parameter, you can specify how many of the generated sequences should be used for the validation sample.

Since creating a transformer model is energy-consuming, *aifeducation*
allows you to estimate its ecological impact with the help of the Python library 'codecarbon.' Thus, the `sustain_track` parameter is set to `TRUE` by default.
If you use the sustainability tracker, you must provide the three-letter code for the country in which your computer is located (e.g. "CAN" for Canada, "DEU" for Germany). You can find a list of these codes on
[Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_3166-1_alpha-3). This is because different countries use different sources and techniques for generating energy, resulting in a specific impact on CO₂ emissions. For the USA and Canada, you can also specify a region by setting `sustain_region`. Please refer to the 'codecarbon' documentation for more information.

If you are working on a machine with a small memory capacity, please reduce the batch size significantly.
Once the training is complete, you can save the entire model using the `save_to_disk` function.


```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
save_to_disk(
  object = base_model_bert,
  dir_path = "examples",
  folder_name = "example_base_model_bert"
)
```

To use the model, load it with

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
base_model_bert <- load_from_disk("examples/example_base_model_bert")
```

To use the model for the fill-mask task, call the `fill_mask` method

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
base_model_bert$fill_mask(
  masked_text = "This is a [MASK] movie.",
  n_solutions = 5
)
```

Here, you can provide a text containing a masked token to indicate the gap that the model should fill.
In return, you will receive the logits, the token ID and the specific token that the model suggests replacing the mask token with.

You get a short summary of an object of this class with `print`.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
print(base_model_bert)
```

## 3.4 Analyzing a BaseModel

If you would like to investigate a base model further, you can use specific methods for this purpose.

**Training History**

The training history from the last training session can be displayed as follows:

```{r, include = TRUE, eval=TRUE, fig.cap=paste0("Figure ",running_num_figures,": Example of a Training History for a BaseModel.")}
base_model_bert$plot_training_history(
  ind_best_model = TRUE
)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
running_num_figures <- running_num_figures + 1
```

**Sustainability of Training**

To explore the ecological impact of training and fine-tuning a model, call  `get_sustainability_data("training")`.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
# We use t() to improve the readability of the table
t(base_model_bert$get_sustainability_data("training"))
```

The resulting table provides detailed information on every training run, with active sustainability tracking.

**Sustainability of Inference**

The ecological impact of the training is important, as are the energy consumption and CO2 emissions during inference. You can estimate the ecological impact by calling the `estimate_sustainability_inference_fill_mask` method.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
base_model_bert$estimate_sustainability_inference_fill_mask(
  text_dataset = data_set_reviews_text,
  n = 30,
  sustain_iso_code = "DEU",
  sustain_region = NULL,
  sustain_interval = 15,
  sustain_log_level = "error",
  trace = TRUE
)
```

Here, you can provide a text dataset which forms the basis for estimating energy consumption during a fill-mask task. You determine the number of texts to be used with `n`. The results of each run can be accessed using the command `get_sustainability_data("inference")`.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
# We use t() to improve the readability of the table
t(base_model_bert$get_sustainability_data("inference"))
```

**FLOPS Estimates**

Another important value is the total number of FLOPS during training. These are
estimated during every training run. With `get_flops_estimates` you receive a
table. 

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
# We use t() to improve the readability of the table
t(base_model_bert$get_flops_estimates())
```

Currently, only an architecture-based approach is available. The number of FLOPS is not counted directly. Instead, it is estimated approximately. The 'flops_bp_1' column describes the number of FLOPS for all forward and backward passes.

Kaplan et al. (2020, p. 7) propose that, as a rule of thumb, the backward pass has FLOPS equal to those of the forward pass multiplied by 2. The resulting FLOPS for all forward and backward passes in a training run are shown in column 'flops_bp_2'.

None of the columns include computations for a validation or test sample.

## 3.5 Creating a BaseModel from Hugging Face

If you would like to use a pre-trained model from Hugging Face, you can create a base model as follows:

- Choose a model on Hugging Face. Ensure that the model's architecture is supported by *aifeducation.*
- Download the relevant files (model and tokeniser) into a folder on your machine.
- Create an empty base model for the corresponding architecture.
- Call the method `create_from_hf` and provide the path to the folder where you stored the model and tokenizer.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = FALSE}
base_model_bert_hf <- BaseModelBert$new()
base_model_bert_hf$create_from_hf(
  model_dir = "examples/bert_uncased",
  tokenizer_dir = "examples/bert_uncased"
)
```

You can now use the model in the same way as all the other base models in *aifedcuation.* For example, you can train the model as described above, or use it as the basis for a `TextEmbeddingModel`.

# 4 Text Embedding Models

## 4.1 Introduction

The text embedding model transforms raw text into numerical representations. 
To create a new model, you need a base model with the ability to understand natural language. A text embedding model is stored as an object of the class `TextEmbeddingModel`.

In *aifeducation*, the process of converting raw text into numerical data is a separate step from downstream tasks such as classification. This reduces computational time on low-performance machines. By separating text embedding from other tasks, the embedding only needs to be calculated once and can be used for different tasks simultaneously. Another advantage is that training the downstream tasks involves only the tasks themselves and not the parameters of the embedding model, making training less time-consuming and decreasing computational intensity. Finally, this approach enables long documents to be analysed by applying the same algorithm to different parts of a text.

The text embedding model provides a unified interface. After creating the model using different methods, it is always handled in the same way.

## 4.2 Create a Text Embedding Model

First, you must choose the base model on which your new text embedding model will be built. 
To illustrate its use, we apply a pre-trained model from [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/) called [EuroBERT-210m](https://huggingface.co/EuroBERT/EuroBERT-210m).It is based on the work by Boizard et al. (2025). 
Download all the files into a new folder. We will store the model here: `"examples/EuroBERT-210m"`.

As described in Section 3, we first load the base model.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
base_model_eurobert <- BaseModelEuroBert$new()
base_model_eurobert$create_from_hf(
  model_dir = "examples/EuroBERT-210m",
  tokenizer_dir = "examples/EuroBERT-210m"
)
```

Now, we can create the `TextEmbeddingModel`. First, we need to choose a value for both `chunks` and `overlap`.
Using a transformer model for text embedding is not a problem, as long as your text does not contain more tokens than the transformer can process. This maximum value is set in the transformer's configuration (see section 3.3). We can request the maximum sequence length of a base model with:

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
total_max_seq_len <- base_model_eurobert$get_max_seq_len()
total_max_seq_len
```

If the text produces more tokens than can be accommodated, the last ones are ignored. In some instances, you may wish to analyse long texts. Reducing the text to the first tokens (e.g. the first 512 tokens) could result in a problematic loss of information in these situations. To deal with this, you can configure a text embedding model in *aifecuation* to split long texts into several chunks, each of which is processed by the base model. The maximum number of chunks is set with the `chunks` parameter. 

Since transformers can account for context, it may be useful to interconnect every chunk in order to incorporate context into the calculations. This can be achieved using the `overlap` parameter, which determines how many tokens from the end of a prior chunk should be added to the next.

To support you in this decision, the tokenizer of a base model can calculate how many chunks are needed to cover a specific quantile of texts in full. We will illustrate this with an example. Let's assume that we want an overlap of 128 tokens (`token_overlap`) between each chunk. Our `BaseModel` can process a maximum of `r total_max_seq_len` tokens. In this example, we use 512 tokens as the basis for each text embedding.
Passing these values to the `calc_quantiles` method of the tokenizer reveals the following quantiles:

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
chunk_quantile <- base_model_eurobert$Tokenizer$calc_quantiles(
  text_dataset = data_set_reviews_text,
  batch_size = 32L,
  seq_len_tokens = 512L,
  token_overlap = 128L,
  trace = FALSE
)
print(chunk_quantile)
max_chunks <- chunk_quantile["99.9%"]
```

To ensure that approximately 90% of texts are fully covered by our text embedding model with the given configuration, we require `r chunk_quantile`[`"90%"`] chunks. To ensure that 99.9% of the text is fully represented, we need `r chunk_quantile["90%"]` chunks. We have chosen the 99.9% quantile, which requires `r chunk_quantile["99.9%"]`. In total, this model can analyse a maximum of `r 512+(chunk_quantile["99.9%"]-1)*(512-128)` tokens of text.

Finally, you need to decide which hidden layer or layers the embeddings should be drawn from. Using the parameters `emb_layer_min` and `emb_layer_max`, you can specify the layers from which the average value for each token should be calculated. Please note that the calculation considers all layers between `emb_layer_min` and `emb_layer_max`. You can request the maximum number of available layers with:

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
num_layers <- base_model_eurobert$get_n_layers()
num_layers
```

In their initial work, Devlin et al. (2019) used the hidden states of different layers for classification. A study by Liu et al. (2019, p. 1078) investigated the performance of models on 16 linguistic tasks and revealed that, for transformers, there is no single best layer; rather, the best layers are located in the middle and up to the two-thirds layer. Thus, we use the following layers:

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
eurobert_min_layer <- floor(0.5 * num_layers)
eurobert_min_layer

eurobert_max_layer <- ceiling(2 / 3 * num_layers)
eurobert_max_layer
```

Using the `emb_pool_type` parameter, you can specify which tokens are used for pooling within each layer. With the "CLS" option, only the CLS token is used. With the "Average" option, all tokens within a layer are averaged, except for padding tokens.

The `emb_insert_mask_tokens` parameter allows you to specify the percentage of tokens to be replaced with the model's masking token. This can improve performance on subsequent tasks. This is because the masked language modelling applied during training does not match the conditions during application, since working with texts outside of training does not require tokens to be masked (Meng et al. 2024, p. 1).

> The vignette [04 Model configuration and training](model_configuration.html)
> provides details on how to configure a text embedding model.

Remember to pass the base model to the parameter called `base_model`.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
tem <- TextEmbeddingModel$new()
tem$configure(
  model_label = "Text Embedding via EuroBert - 210m",
  model_language = "english",
  max_length = 512,
  chunks = max_chunks,
  overlap = 128,
  emb_layer_min = eurobert_min_layer,
  emb_layer_max = eurobert_max_layer,
  emb_pool_type = "Average",
  base_model = base_model_eurobert,
  emb_insert_mask_tokens = 0.15
)
```

Once you have decided on the configuration, you can start using your model.
You can view the number of learnable parameters of the underlying base model.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
tem$BaseModel$count_parameter()
```

Another important value is the number of features that can be requested using the method `get_n_features`.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
tem$get_n_features()
```

This number describes the number of dimensions used to characterise a text embedding. In other words, it is the number of dimensions used to characterise the content of every piece of text. This value is important because it determines the complexity that a classifier or feature extractor has to deal with. Some parameters of classifiers and feature extractors depend on this value. We will elaborate on this at the relevant point for the different models.

The `print` function provides a brief summary of an object of this class.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
print(tem)
```


## 4.3 Transforming Raw Texts into Embedded Texts

To transform raw text into a numeric representation, simply use the `embed_large` method of your model. To do this, you must provide a `LargeDataSetForText` to `text_dataset.` Using the sample data from section 2.3, we can use the movie reviews as the raw text.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
review_embeddings <- tem$embed_large(
  text_dataset = data_set_reviews_text,
  trace = TRUE
)
```

The method `embed_large` creates an object of the class `LargeDataSetForTextEmbeddings.` This is simply a data set consisting of the embeddings of each text. The embeddings are an array, where the first dimension refers to specific texts, the second to chunks/sequences and the third to features.

You can inspect the data set with `print`.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
print(review_embeddings)
```

You now have the input to train a new classifier or apply a pre-trained one for predicting categories/classes with the embedded texts.
The next chapter will show you how to use these classifiers. But before we begin, we will demonstrate how to save and load your model.

## 4.4 Saving and Loading Embedded Texts

Since the process of transforming raw text into text embeddings is time-consuming, we recommend saving them to disk in order to use the embeddings for further tasks and analysis.
To do this, simply call the function save_to_disk, as shown below.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
save_to_disk(
  object = review_embeddings,
  dir_path = "examples",
  folder_name = "imdb_movie_reviews"
)
```

To load the embeddings you can call the function `load_from_disk`.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
review_embeddings <- load_from_disk("examples/imdb_movie_reviews")
```

## 4.5 Saving and Loading Text Embedding Models

In *aifeducation*, saving a created text embedding model is very easy using the function `save_to_disk`. This function provides a unique interface for all text embedding models. To save your work, pass your model to the `object` parameter and the directory in which to save the model to the `dir_path` parameter. You can also specify the name of the folder that should be created in that directory to store the model using the parameter `folder_name.`

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
save_to_disk(
  object = tem,
  dir_path = "examples",
  folder_name = "eurobert_te_model"
)
```

In this example, the model is saved in the folder `"examples/eurobert_te_model"`. To load your model, call the `load_from_disk` function.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
tem <- load_from_disk("examples/eurobert_te_model")
```

## 4.6 Sustainability

If the underlying model was trained with an active sustainability tracker (see sections 3.2 and 3.3), you can retrieve a table showing the energy consumption, CO₂ emissions and hardware used during training by calling `BaseModel$get_sustainability_data("training")`. In our example, this would be `tem$BaseModel$get_sustainability_data("training")`.

## 4.7 Training History

You can call a special method to view the training history of the underlying base model.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = FALSE}
tem$BaseModel$plot_training_history(
  ind_best_model = TRUE
)
```

Please note that this plot is unavailable for this example, as the necessary data is not directly accessible for this model on Hugging Face. However, if you train a model with this package, the training history is always saved.

# 5 Overview Classifiers

Classifiers are built on top of a `TextEmbeddingModel`. They use the embedded texts
produced by these models and predict classes/categories. You can build your own classifier with the help of two components.

First, you choose a core model. It determines
where different layers are located and how the outputs of the different layers are
combined into the final output of the model. 
  
![Figure `r running_num_figures`: Basic Architecture of a Sequential Classifier](core_arch_sequential.png){width="100%"}
```{r, include = FALSE}
running_num_figures <- running_num_figures + 1
```

The sequential architecture (Figure `r running_num_figures-1`) provides models where the input is passed to a specific number 
of layers step by step. All layers are grouped by their kind into stacks.

In contrast, the parallel architecture (Figure `r running_num_figures`) offers a model where 
an input is passed to different types of layers separately. At the end the outputs 
are combined to create the final output of the whole model. 

![Figure `r running_num_figures`: Basic Architecture of a Parallel Classifier](core_arch_parallel.png){width="100%"}
```{r, include = FALSE}
running_num_figures <- running_num_figures + 1
```

You can find the name of the used core model in the name of the classifiers. For
example `TEClassifierSequential` uses a *sequential* core model while
`TEClassifierParallel` uses a *parallel* core model.

In general, all layers within a core model allow further customization allowing you
to build a high number of different models.
  
> A detailed description of all layers can be found in vignette [A01 Layers and Stack of Layers](https://fberding.github.io/aifeducation/articles/a01_layers_and_stack_layers.html):

Second, you can choose how the core model is used for classification. At the moment
a probability and metric based classifier is possible. 

- **Probability Based Classifiers:**  Probability classifiers are used to predict a 
  probability distribution for different classes/categories. This is the standard case most common
  in literature.
- **Prototype Based Classifiers:** Prototype based classifiers are a kind of metric
  based classifiers. Here the classifiers do not predict a probability distribution. Instead
  it calculates a prototype for every class/category and measures the distance
  between a case and all prototypes. The class/category of the prototype with the smallest distance
  to the case is assigned to that case. In contrast to the probability classifiers
  these models can handle classes/categories that were not part of the training. For more details
  please refer to section 7.

The training of a classifier consists of two stages. The first stage aims to
estimate the performance of the model while the second stage trains the model
for application.
  
For performance estimation, training splits the data into several chunks
based on cross-fold validation. The number of folds is set with
`data_folds`. In every case, one fold is not used for training and
serves as a *test* sample. The remaining data is used to create a
*training* and a *validation* sample. The percentage of cases within
each fold used as a validation sample is determined with
`data_val_size`. This sample is used to determine the state of the model
that generalizes best. All performance values saved in the trained
classifier refer to the test sample. This data has never been used
during training and provides a more realistic estimation of a
classifier's performance.  
  
Since *aifedcuation* tries to address the special needs in educational
and social science, some special training steps are integrated for all models.

-   **Synthetic Cases:** In case of imbalanced data, it is recommended
    to augment your data. Before training, a number of new units
    is created via different techniques. Currently you can request
    the *K-Nearest Neighbor OveRsampling Approach (KNNOR)*
    developed by Islam et al. (2022). The aim is to create new
    cases that fill the gap to the majority class. Multi-class problems
    are reduced to a two class problem (class under investigation vs.
    all others) for generating these units. If the technique allows to
    set the number of neighbors during generation, you can configure the
    data generation with `sc_min_k` and `sc_max_k`. The synthetic cases
    for every class are generated for all *k* between `sc_min_k` and
    `sc_max_k`. Every *k* contributes proportionally to the synthetic
    cases.

-   **Pseudo-Labeling:** This technique is relevant if you have labeled
    target data and a large number of unlabeled target data. The idea is to integrate
    the unlabeled into training to increase performance and to avoid high costs by
    labeling a high number of cases manually. With the
    different parameters starting with `pl_`, you can configure the
    process of pseudo-labeling. Implementation of pseudo-labeling is
    based on Cascante-Bonilla et al. (2020). To apply pseudo-labeling,
    you have to set `use_pl=TRUE`. `pl_max=1.00`, `pl_anchor=1.00`, and
    `pl_min=0.00` are used to describe the certainty of a prediction. 0
    refers to random guessing while 1 refers to perfect certainty.
    `pl_anchor` is used as a reference value. The distance to
    `pl_anchor` is calculated for every case. Then, they are sorted with
    an increasing distance from `pl_anchor`. The proportion of added
    pseudo-labeled data into training increases with every step. The
    maximum number of steps is determined with `pl_max_steps`. Cases close to
    `pl_anchor` are included first.

Figure `r running_num_figures` illustrates the training loop for the cases that all options
are set to `TRUE`.

![Figure `r running_num_figures`: Overview of the Steps to Perform a Classification](classif_fig_05.png){width="100%"}  

```{r, include = FALSE}
running_num_figures <- running_num_figures + 1
```  

The example stated in the Figure applies the generation of synthetic cases and the
algorithm proposed by Cascante-Bonilla et al. (2020). For every fold,
the training starts with generating synthetic cases to fill the gap
between the classes and the majority class. After this, an initial
training of the classifiers starts. The trained classifier is used to
predict pseudo-labels for the unlabeled part of the data and adds 20% of
the cases with the highest certainty for their pseudo-labels to the
training data set. Now new synthetic cases are generated based on both
the labeled data and the newly added pseudo-labeled data. The classifier
is re-initialized and trained again. After training, the classifier
predicts the potential labels of *all* originally unlabeled data and
adds 40% of the pseudo-labeled data to the training data with the
highest certainty. Again, new synthetic cases are generated on both the
labeled and added pseudo-labeled data. The model is again re-initialized
and trained again until the maximum number of steps for pseudo labeling
(`pl_max_steps`) is reached. After this, the logarithm is restated for
the next fold until the number of folds (`data_folds`) is reached. All
of these steps are only used to estimate the performance of the
classifier to evaluate for unknown data.

The last phase of the training begins after the last fold. In the final
training, the data set is split only into a training and validation set
without a test set to provide the maximum amount of data for the best
performance in final training. All configurations of the performance 
estimation phase are used in the final training phase.
  
> Please note that creating, training, and Predicting works for all types of classifiers 
> as described in the chapters below.

# 6 Probability Based Classifiers

## 6.1 Creation

To demonstrate how to create a classifier, we will use an example of a `TEClassifierSequential` classifier. Using the sample data from Section 2.3 and the text embeddings from Section 4.3, creating a new classifier might look like this:

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
classifier <- TEClassifierSequential$new()
classifier$configure(
  label = "Classifier for Estimating a Postive or Negative Rating of Movie Reviews",
  text_embeddings = review_embeddings,
  feature_extractor = NULL,
  target_levels = c("neg", "pos"),
  skip_connection_type = "ResidualGate",
  cls_pooling_features = 20,
  cls_pooling_type = "WeightedAverageTimes",
  cls_head_type = "Regular",
  cls_input_normalize="PowerNorm",
  final_normalization_type="RMSNorm",
  feat_act_fct = "None",
  feat_size = 128,
  feat_bias = FALSE,
  feat_dropout = 0.05,
  feat_parametrizations = "None",
  feat_normalization_type = "RMSNorm",
  ng_conv_act_fct = "GELU",
  ng_conv_n_layers = 0,
  ng_conv_ks_min = 1,
  ng_conv_ks_max = 2,
  ng_conv_bias = FALSE,
  ng_conv_dropout = 0.40,
  ng_conv_parametrizations = "None",
  ng_conv_normalization_type = "RMSNorm",
  ng_conv_residual_type = "ResidualGate",
  dense_act_fct = "GELU",
  dense_n_layers = 3,
  dense_dropout = 0.40,
  dense_bias = FALSE,
  dense_parametrizations = "None",
  dense_normalization_type = "RMSNorm",
  dense_residual_type = "ResidualGate",
  rec_act_fct = "Tanh",
  rec_n_layers = 0,
  rec_type = "GRU",
  rec_bidirectional = FALSE,
  rec_dropout = 0.2,
  rec_bias = FALSE,
  rec_parametrizations = "None",
  rec_normalization_type = "RMSNorm",
  rec_residual_type = "ResidualGate",
  tf_act_fct = "SwiGLU",
  tf_dense_dim = ceiling(2.67 * 384),
  tf_n_layers = 0,
  tf_dropout_rate_1 = 0.1,
  tf_dropout_rate_2 = 0.3,
  tf_attention_type = "MultiHead",
  tf_positional_type = "absolute",
  tf_num_heads = 4,
  tf_bias = FALSE,
  tf_parametrizations = "None",
  tf_normalization_type = "RMSNorm",
  tf_normalization_position = "Post",
  tf_residual_type = "ResidualGate"
)
```

As with the text embedding model, you should provide a label (`label` ) for your new classifier. 
For the text embeddings, you must provide a `LargeDataSetForTextEmbeddings`.
This data set is created using a `TextEmbeddingModel`, as described in section 4. Here, we continue our example by using the embeddings produced by our BERT model.

The `target_levels` take the categories/classes that your classifier should predict. These can be numbers or words.

>If you would like to use ordinal data, it is very important that you provide the classes/categories in the correct order. In other words, categories/classes representing a 'higher' level must be stated after those representing a 'lower' level. If you provide the wrong order, the performance indices will be invalid. The order does not matter for nominal data.

Using the `feature_extractor`, you can reduce the number of features in your text embeddings before passing them to the classifier. You can read more about this in Section 7.

You can use the other parameters to define the complexity and capabilities of your model.
Descriptions of the different models can be found in [A01 Layers and Stack of Layers](https://fberding.github.io/aifeducation/articles/a01_layers_and_stack_layers.html). 

Please note that you must choose the parameter `feat_size` depending on the number of features of the underlying text embedding model. You can obtain this number by calling the `get_n_features` method of the text embedding model used. In our example, this would be:

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
tem$get_n_features()
```

The value of `feat_size` should be equal to or less than this value since this layer tries to compress the text embeddings into fewer dimensions. While this reduces the number of parameters for all subsequent layers and decreases training and usage time, it may result in information loss.
You can experiment with this value to strike a balance between speed and performance. 
A study by Takeshita et al. (2025) shows that randomly dropping 50% of the dimensions leads only to a minor decrease in performance in classification tasks. Thus, this value can serve as a rule of thumb for determining this parameter. 
In our example, we only have a very limited number of samples. Therefore, we reduce the number of features even further.

In addition, the value of the parameter `cls_pooling_features` should be equal to or less than the value of feat_size. The value of `cls_pooling_features` determines how many of the resulting features are used for classification. Therefore, this value acts as a filter. This value is only relevant if your pooling method does not include the word 'Times'.

> The vignette [04 Model configuration and training](model_configuration.html)
> provides details on how to configure a classifier.

Since we have a small data set and a short sequence, we set all layers to 0 (`tf_n_layers`,`rec_n_layers`,`ng_conv_n_layers`), except the dense layers. Here, we use 3 (`dense_n_layers = 3`).

As pooling method we use weighted average over time (`cls_pooling_type="WeightedAverageTimes"`). In other words, the values of a specific feature dimension are averaged over all tokens and chunks, and the weights are learnt during training. 

In this example, we use a regular classification head (`cls_head_type = "Regular"`), where all neurons in the previous layer are connected to all classes. 
Li et al. [(2020)](https://doi.org/10.1109/TIP.2020.2990277) proposed a special classification head (`cls_head_type = "PairwiseOrthogonal"`). This layer enables each neuron to establish a connection with only one class. To improve performance with high rates of dropout in the previous layers, you can add a dense layer before the classification head (`cls_head_type = "PairwiseOrthogonalDense"`).

You receive a short summary of the classifier by calling `print`.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
print(classifier)
```

Once you have created a new classifier, you can start the training process. 
You can view the number of learnable parameters of your model using the following method:

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
classifier$count_parameter()
```

## 6.2 Training

To start training your classifier, call the `train` method and provide the text embeddings to `data_embeddings` and the categories/classes as target data to `data_targets`. Please note that data_targets expects a *named* `factor` where the names correspond to the IDs of the corresponding text embeddings. Text embeddings and target data that cannot be matched are omitted from training.

```{r classifier$train, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
classifier$train(
  data_embeddings = review_embeddings,
  data_targets = review_labels,
  data_folds = 10,
  data_val_size = 0.25,
  loss_balance_class_weights = TRUE,
  loss_balance_sequence_length = TRUE,
  loss_cls_fct_name = "AEMLoss",
  #loss_cls_fct_name = "FocalLoss",
  use_sc = TRUE,
  sc_method = "knnor",
  sc_min_k = 1,
  sc_max_k = 10,
  use_pl = FALSE,
  pl_max_steps = 3,
  pl_max = 1.00,
  pl_anchor = 1.00,
  pl_min = 0.00,
  sustain_track = TRUE,
  sustain_iso_code = "DEU",
  sustain_region = NULL,
  sustain_interval = 15,
  sustain_log_level = "error",
  epochs = 2000,
  batch_size = 128,
  trace = TRUE,
  ml_trace = 1,
  log_dir = NULL,
  log_write_interval = 10,
  n_cores = auto_n_cores(),
  lr_rate = 0.0,
  lr_min = 0.0,
  lr_scheduler = "Linear",
  lr_epochs = 30,
  lr_warm_up_ratio = 0.10,
  optimizer = "AdamW",
  amp = TRUE,
  comp_use=TRUE,
  comp_mode="reduce-overhead"
)
```

You can modify the training process further by using different arguments.
Setting `loss_balance_class_weights` to TRUE adjusts the weights of the classes/categories according to the 'Inverse Class Frequency' method. This option should be activated if you are dealing with imbalanced data.

Enabling the `loss_balance_sequence_length` option can improve performance when dealing with texts of different lengths with imbalanced frequencies. When this option is enabled, the loss is adjusted according to the 'Inverse Class Frequency' method, based on the absolute frequencies of the lengths of your texts.

The parameter `epochs` determines the maximum number of epochs. During training, the model with the most balanced accuracy is saved and used.

The value of the parameter `batch_size` determines the number of cases to be processed simultaneously. It is a very important parameter that significantly impacts the model's performance due to the generalisation gap (Keskar et al. 2017, p. 2). This describes the observation that models trained with a large batch size tend to perform poorly on test data sets compared to those trained with a small batch size (Keskar et al. 2017, p. 3). 
A study by Masters and Luschi (2018) suggests how to determine an optimal batch size when using SGD as an optimizer. Their study shows that smaller batch sizes offer more stable and reliable training, while also achieving better generalisation performance. Batch sizes between 4 and 32 lead to the best performance. In practice, however, we need large batch sizes to efficiently use computer hardware and save time and energy. Therefore, the aim is to use the largest possible batch size while achieving good generalisation performance. To achieve this, use large batch sizes and large dropout values. Please note that there are exceptions to this rule. In the context of contrastive learning, for example, higher batch sizes tend to generate better generalisation performance (Chen et al. 2020).For more details please refer to the vignette [04 Model configuration and training](model_configuration.html)

We set `lr_rate` and `lr_min` to `0.0` to request an automatic calculation of a suitable learning rate.

To speed up computations, we activate Automatic Mixed Precision (AMP) with gradient scaling by setting `amp = TRUE`. In general, we recommend activating mixed precision. If you encounter any problems, turn this option off.

Since training a neural net is energy-consuming, *aifeducation*
allows you to estimate its ecological impact with the help of the Python library 'codecarbon.' Thus, the `sustain_track` parameter is set to `TRUE` by default.
If you use the sustainability tracker, you must provide the three-letter code for the country in which your computer is located (e.g. "CAN" for Canada, "DEU" for Germany). You can find a list of these codes on
[Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_3166-1_alpha-3). This is because different countries use different sources and techniques for generating energy, resulting in a specific impact on CO₂ emissions. For the USA and Canada, you can also specify a region by setting `sustain_region`. Please refer to the 'codecarbon' documentation for more information.

Finally, the `trace` and `ml_trace` options allow you to control how much information about the training process is printed to the console.

Please note that training the classifier can take some time. 
If options such as generating synthetic cases (`use_sc`) or pseudo-labelling (`use_pl`) are disabled, the training process is shorter.

After performance estimation, the final training of the classifier uses all available data. In other words, the test sample is left empty.

To visualise the progress of the training, you can request a plot showing how important performance measures develop over epochs.
You can choose from the following measures: classifier's loss (`"loss"`), accuracy (`"accuracy"`), balanced accuracy (`"balanced_accuracy"`), and average iota (`"avg_iota"`). Set `final_training=FALSE` to request the mean values of all the folds used during the performance estimation phase.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE, fig.cap = paste0("Figure ",running_num_figures,": Training History of a Classifier during Performance Estimation Stage (loss)"),fig.align="center"}
classifier$plot_training_history(
  final_training = FALSE,
  pl_step = NULL,
  measure = "loss",
  ind_best_model = FALSE,
  ind_selected_model = TRUE,
  x_min = NULL,
  x_max = NULL,
  y_min = NULL,
  y_max = NULL,
  add_min_max = FALSE,
  text_size = 10
)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
running_num_figures <- running_num_figures + 1
```



Figure `r running_num_figures-1` shows the development of the loss averaged across all folds. In general, the training curve should decrease to zero. The curves for the validation and test samples should also decrease, but then start to increase after a certain point. The rectangles indicate the state of the model selected as the best during a fold.

Since there are some measures that provide a better post-hoc analysis than the loss, you can request further plots. The following plot shows the development of the average iota for all categories/classes.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE, fig.cap = paste0("Figure ",running_num_figures,": Training History of a Classifier during Performance Estimation Stage (iota)"),fig.align="center"}
classifier$plot_training_history(
  final_training = FALSE,
  pl_step = NULL,
  measure = "avg_iota",
  ind_best_model = FALSE,
  ind_selected_model = TRUE,
  x_min = NULL,
  x_max = NULL,
  y_min = NULL,
  y_max = NULL,
  add_min_max = FALSE,
  text_size = 10
)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
running_num_figures <- running_num_figures + 1
```

The average iota ranges between 0 and 1 and indicates how well the predictions represent the true values. Higher values indicate better performance. Since measures such as average iota are based on discrete values that can fluctuate significantly, you can plot a smoothed version of average iota, which is more precise.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE, fig.cap = paste0("Figure ",running_num_figures,": Training History of a Classifier during Performance Estimation Stage (smoothed iota)"),fig.align="center"}
classifier$plot_training_history(
  final_training = FALSE,
  pl_step = NULL,
  measure = "s_avg_iota",
  ind_best_model = FALSE,
  ind_selected_model = TRUE,
  x_min = NULL,
  x_max = NULL,
  y_min = NULL,
  y_max = NULL,
  add_min_max = FALSE,
  text_size = 10
)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
running_num_figures <- running_num_figures + 1
```

To view the final training stage, set `final_training` to `TRUE`, as shown in the following figures. 

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE, fig.cap = paste0("Figure ",running_num_figures,": Training History of a Classifier during Final Training Stage (loss)"),fig.align="center"}
classifier$plot_training_history(
  final_training = TRUE,
  pl_step = NULL,
  measure = "loss",
  ind_best_model = FALSE,
  ind_selected_model = TRUE,
  x_min = NULL,
  x_max = NULL,
  y_min = NULL,
  y_max = NULL,
  add_min_max = FALSE,
  text_size = 10
)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
running_num_figures <- running_num_figures + 1
```

The dotted line indicates the final model state. Please note that this state is not always the one with the lowest validation loss value, because the best model is selected by applying several criteria in a hierarchical order. The first criterion is the model's performance in terms of the smoothed average iota The second criterion is the loss.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE, fig.cap = paste0("Figure ",running_num_figures,": Training History of a Classifier during Final Training Stage (iota)"),fig.align="center"}
classifier$plot_training_history(
  final_training = TRUE,
  pl_step = NULL,
  measure = "avg_iota",
  ind_best_model = FALSE,
  ind_selected_model = TRUE,
  x_min = NULL,
  x_max = NULL,
  y_min = NULL,
  y_max = NULL,
  add_min_max = FALSE,
  text_size = 10
)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
running_num_figures <- running_num_figures + 1
```

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE, fig.cap = paste0("Figure ",running_num_figures,": Training History of a Classifier during Final Training Stage (smoothed iota)"),fig.align="center"}
classifier$plot_training_history(
  final_training = TRUE,
  pl_step = NULL,
  measure = "s_avg_iota",
  ind_best_model = FALSE,
```
