```

To gain a deeper insight into the training process, you can request a plot visualising the learning rate calculation. Please note that this plot is only available if you have set either `lr_rate` or `lr_min` to `0.0`.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE, fig.cap = paste0("Figure ",running_num_figures,": Analysis of Different Learning Rates"),fig.align="center"}
classifier$plot_learning_rate()
```

The bars in the plot show the percentage increase or decrease in loss compared to the initial loss. The values express the percentage change from the initial loss.
A decrease is desirable. The points on the plot show a smoothed distribution of the loss. 
All calculations for selecting good maximum and minimum learning rates are based on the smoothed data. 
The automatic calculation selects the learning rate from the range of learning rates that leads to the greatest decrease in loss. The maximum learning rate is set at the point where the decrease in loss turns. The minimum learning rate is set to the rate that results in the smallest reduction in loss. Depending on the learning rate scheduler, other points may be chosen.


```{r, include = FALSE}
running_num_figures <- running_num_figures + 1
```

## 6.3 Performance Evaluation

Once training is complete, you can evaluate the performance of the classifier. For each fold, the classifier is applied to the test sample and the results are compared to the true categories/classes. As the test sample is never part of the training set, all performance measures provide a more realistic idea of the classifier's performance.

To help researchers judge the quality of the predictions,
*aifeducation* uses several measures and concepts from content analysis. These are:

-   Iota Concept of the Second Generation (Berding & Pargmann 2022).
-   Krippendorff's Alpha (Krippendorff 2019).
-   Percentage Agreement.
-   Gwet's AC1/AC2 (Gwet 2014).
-   Kendall's coefficient of concordance W.
-   Cohen's Kappa unweighted (Cohen 1960).
-   Cohen's Kappa with equal weights (Cohen 1968).
-   Cohen's Kappa with squared weights (Cohen 1968).
-   Fleiss' Kappa for multiple raters without exact estimation (Fleiss 1971).

You can access the mean values across all folds via `reliability$test_metric_mean`. In our example, this would be:

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
classifier$reliability$test_metric_mean
```

An addition, standard measures from machine learning are reported. These
are

-   Precision
-   Recall
-   F1-Score

You can access these values as follows:

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
classifier$reliability$standard_measures_mean
```

To analyse the quality of the training across all folds, you can request an additional box plot. The figure below shows the performance that the classifier achieved. 

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE, fig.cap = paste0("Figure ",running_num_figures,": Box Plot of Performance Measures"),fig.align="center"}
classifier$plot_reliability_distribution(measures="all")
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
running_num_figures <- running_num_figures + 1
```

Finally, you can plot a coding stream scheme to show how cases in different classes are labelled. 

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE, fig.cap = paste0("Figure ",running_num_figures,": Coding Stream of the Classifier"),fig.align="center"}
classifier$plot_coding_stream()
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
running_num_figures <- running_num_figures + 1
```

Evaluating the performance of a classifier is a complex task that goes beyond the scope of this vignette. If you would like to delve deeper into this topic, we recommend consulting the cited literature on content analysis and machine learning.

## 6.4 Sustainability

If the classifier was trained with an active sustainability tracker, you can retrieve sustainability information by calling 
`classifier$get_sustainability_data()`.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
# We use t() to improve the readability of the table
t(classifier$get_sustainability_data())
```

## 6.5 Saving and Loading a Classifier

The saving and loading process follows the same pattern as for the other objects.
*aifeducation*. You can save the classifier by calling the `save_to_disk` function.
In our example, this might look like this:

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
save_to_disk(
  object = classifier,
  dir_path = "examples",
  folder_name = "cls_imdb_movie_reviews"
)
```

The classifier is saved to `examples/cls_imdb_movie_reviews`. To load
the model call `load_from_disk`.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
classifier <- load_from_disk("examples/cls_imdb_movie_reviews")
```

## 6.6 Predicting New Data

If you would like to apply your classifier to new data, two steps are necessary. First, you must transform the raw text into a numerical representation using *exactly* the same text embedding model that was used to train your classifier (see Section 4). In the case of our example classifier, we use our BERT model.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
# If our model is not loaded
tem <- load_from_disk("examples/eurobert_te_model")

# Create a numerical representation of the text
review_embeddings <- tem$embed_large(
  text_dataset = data_set_reviews_text,
  trace = TRUE
)
```

To transform raw text into a numeric representation, simply pass the text to the `embed_large` method of the loaded model. The raw text should be an object of the class `LargeDataSetForText`. To create such a data set, please refer to Section 2.

The resulting object can then be passed to the `predict` method of our classifier to obtain predictions together with an estimate of certainty for each class/category.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
# If your classifier is not loaded
classifier <- load_from_disk("examples/cls_imdb_movie_reviews")

# predict the classes of new texts
predicted_categories <- classifier$predict(
  newdata = review_embeddings,
  batch_size = 32
)

# Show predicted categories
head(predicted_categories)

# Count frequencies
table(predicted_categories$expected_category)
```

Once the prediction has been made by the classifier, the estimated categories/classes are stored as 'predicted_categories'. This object is a `data.frame` containing text IDs in the rows and the probabilities of the different categories/classes in the columns. The final column, named 'expected_category', represents the category assigned to a text with the highest probability.

These estimates can be used in further analyses employing common methods from the educational and social sciences, such as correlation analysis, regression analysis, structural equation modelling, latent class analysis, and analysis of variance.

Now you are ready to to use *aifeducation*. 

# 7 Feature Extractors

## 7.1 Introduction

Another way to improve a model's performance and/or computational speed is to apply a feature extractor. For example, the work of Ganesan et al. (2021) suggests that reducing the hidden size can improve a model's accuracy. In *aifeducation*, a feature extractor is a model that reduces the number of features of given text embeddings before feeding the embeddings as input to a classifier.

The feature extractors implemented in *aifeducation* are auto-encoders that support sequential data and sequences of different lengths. The basic architecture of all the extractors is shown in the following figure.

```{r, include = FALSE}
running_num_figures <- running_num_figures + 1
```

![Figure `r running_num_figures`: Basic architecture of feature extractors](classif_feature_extractor.png){width="100%"}

The learning objective of the feature extractors is to compress information by reducing the number of features to that of the latent space (Frochte 2019, p. 281). In the figure above, this would mean reducing the number of features from eight to four and storing as much information as possible from eight dimensions in four dimensions.
Next, the extractor attempts to reconstruct the original information from the compressed latent space information (Frochte 2019, pp. 280–281). The information is then extended from four dimensions to eight.
After training, the hidden representation of the latent space is used as a pre-processing of the original input.

## 7.2 Creation

In this example, we use the text embeddings from Section 4. You can create a feature extractor as follows: 

```{r, include = TRUE, eval=TRUE}
feature_extractor <- TEFeatureExtractor$new()
feature_extractor$configure(
  label = "Feature extractor for Text Embeddings",
  text_embeddings = review_embeddings,
  features = 384,
  te_n_layers=4,
  method = "Dense",
  orthogonal_method = "matrix_exp",
  noise_factor = 1e-4
)
```

As with the other models, you can use the `label` for the model's label. 
The argument `text_embeddings` takes an object of class `EmbeddedText` or `LargeDataSetForTextEmbeddings.`
This object connects your feature extractor to a specific `TextEmbeddingModel.` In other words, the feature extractor only works with embeddings from the same `TextEmbeddingModel.`

The value of the `features` argument determines the number of features for the compressed representation. The lower the number, the higher the requested compression. This value corresponds to the features of the latent space in the above figure. The `te_n_layers` parameter allows you you to specify the number of layers in the encoder and decoder parts of the model. 

Use this value depending on the number of features of the underlying text embedding model. You can request this value by calling the method `get_n_features` as follows:

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
tem$get_n_features()
```

A study by Takeshita et al. (2025) shows that randomly dropping 50% of the dimensions leads only to a minor decrease in the performance of classification tasks. Therefore, this value can be used as a rule of thumb when determining this parameter. We therefore reduce the number of features to 50% to `r floor(tem$get_n_features()/2)`.

The type of layer that the feature extractor should use is determined by `method`. If you set the method to "LSTM", all layers of the model are long short-term memory layers. If you set the method to "Dense", all layers are standard dense layers.

Regardless of your choice, all models aim to generate a latent space in which the correlation of the features is zero. Thus, all features represent unique information. In addition, all methods except "LSTM" use an orthogonal parameterisation to prevent overfitting and apply parameter sharing. The opposite layers use the same parameters.
For more details, please refer to Ranjan (2019).

You can use the `noise_factor` to add noise during training, causing the feature extractor to perform as a denoising auto-encoder. This can provide more robust generalisations. Since we work with high batch sizes, we set this value to 1e-4.

## 7.3 Training

Training the extractor is identical to that for the other models.
*aifeducation*. Please note that the text embeddings provided to `data_embeddings` must be generated using the same `TextEmbeddingModel` as the embeddings provided when configuring your model.

```{r feature_extractor$train, include = TRUE, eval=TRUE, results='hide'}
feature_extractor$train(
  data_embeddings = review_embeddings,
  data_val_size = 0.25,
  sustain_track = TRUE,
  sustain_iso_code = "DEU",
  sustain_region = NULL,
  sustain_interval = 15,
  sustain_log_level = "error",
  epochs = 8000,
  batch_size = 128,
  lr_rate = 0.0,
  lr_min = 0.0,
  lr_epochs = 30,
  lr_scheduler = "Linear",
  trace = TRUE,
  ml_trace = 1,
  optimizer = "AdamW",
  amp = TRUE,
  lr_warm_up_ratio = 0.10,
  comp_use=TRUE,
  comp_mode="reduce-overhead"
)
```

>In this example, we use the same text embeddings that we use to train the classifier.
>It can be beneficial to use a larger sample of texts when training a `TEFeatureExtractor` to improve performance and/or allow broader application of the feature extractor.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE, fig.cap = paste0("Figure ",running_num_figures,": Analysis of Different Learning Rates"),fig.align="center"}
feature_extractor$plot_learning_rate()
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
running_num_figures <- running_num_figures + 1
```

You can plot the model's training history using:

```{r, include = TRUE, eval=TRUE, fig.cap=paste0("Figure ",running_num_figures,": Training History of a Feature Extractor.")}
feature_extractor$plot_training_history(
  ind_best_model = TRUE
)
```


```{r, include = FALSE}
running_num_figures <- running_num_figures + 1
```

Calling `print` gives you a short summary of the extractor.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
print(feature_extractor)
```

Let us investigate how the feature extractor decreased the correlation between the features.
First we calculate the correlations of the uncompressed embeddings.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
embeddings_converted=review_embeddings$convert_to_EmbeddedText()
correlations=embeddings_converted$calc_feature_correlation()

correlations$effect_sizes$mean
correlations$effect_sizes$sd
```

Now we calculate the compressed embeddings and estimate the correlation
```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
embeddings_compressed=feature_extractor$extract_features_large(
  review_embeddings,
  batch_size = 32L
  )

embeddings_compressed_converted=embeddings_compressed$convert_to_EmbeddedText()
correlations_compressed=embeddings_compressed_converted$calc_feature_correlation()

correlations_compressed$effect_sizes$mean
correlations_compressed$effect_sizes$sd
```

As you can see the correlation significantly decreased. That is, the feature dimension
contain less overlapping information which may lead to a faster and/or better
performance of a classifier. Lets try how training change in the following section. 

## 7.4 Application

Once you have trained your feature extractor, you can use it with any classifier. Simply pass the feature extractor to the `feature_extractor` parameter during the classifier configuration process. Please note that you now have to set the values for `feat_size` and `cls_pooling_features` depending on the number of features of the feature extractor, and *not* depending on the number of features of the text embedding model, since the aim of the feature extractor is to reduce this number. `feat_size` should be equal to or less than the number of features of the feature extractor, and `cls_pooling_features` should be equal to or less than `feat_size`. 
For the classifier described in Section 6, this would look like this:

```{r, include = TRUE, eval=TRUE}
classifier_with_fe <- TEClassifierSequential$new()
classifier_with_fe$configure(
  label = "Classifier for Estimating a Postive or Negative Rating of Movie Reviews",
  text_embeddings = review_embeddings,
  feature_extractor = feature_extractor,
  target_levels = c("neg", "pos"),
  skip_connection_type = "ResidualGate",
  cls_pooling_features = 20,
  cls_pooling_type = "WeightedAverageTimes",
  cls_head_type = "Regular",
  cls_input_normalize="PowerNorm",
  final_normalization_type="RMSNorm",
  feat_act_fct = "None",
  feat_size = 128,
  feat_bias = FALSE,
  feat_dropout = 0.05,
  feat_parametrizations = "None",
  feat_normalization_type = "RMSNorm",
  ng_conv_act_fct = "GELU",
  ng_conv_n_layers = 0,
  ng_conv_ks_min = 1,
  ng_conv_ks_max = 2,
  ng_conv_bias = FALSE,
  ng_conv_dropout = 0.40,
  ng_conv_parametrizations = "None",
  ng_conv_normalization_type = "RMSNorm",
  ng_conv_residual_type = "ResidualGate",
  dense_act_fct = "GELU",
  dense_n_layers = 3,
  dense_dropout = 0.40,
  dense_bias = FALSE,
  dense_parametrizations = "None",
  dense_normalization_type = "RMSNorm",
  dense_residual_type = "ResidualGate",
  rec_act_fct = "Tanh",
  rec_n_layers = 0,
  rec_type = "GRU",
  rec_bidirectional = FALSE,
  rec_dropout = 0.2,
  rec_bias = FALSE,
  rec_parametrizations = "None",
  rec_normalization_type = "RMSNorm",
  rec_residual_type = "ResidualGate",
  tf_act_fct = "SwiGLU",
  tf_dense_dim = ceiling(2.67 * 384),
  tf_n_layers = 0,
  tf_dropout_rate_1 = 0.1,
  tf_dropout_rate_2 = 0.3,
  tf_attention_type = "MultiHead",
  tf_positional_type = "absolute",
  tf_num_heads = 4,
  tf_bias = FALSE,
  tf_parametrizations = "None",
  tf_normalization_type = "RMSNorm",
  tf_normalization_position = "Post",
  tf_residual_type = "ResidualGate"
)
```

That's all. You can now use and train the classifier in the same way as before, without a feature extractor. You don't even need to save and load the feature extractor manually. This is done automatically for all classifiers.

```{r classifier_with_fe$train, include = TRUE, eval=TRUE}
classifier_with_fe$train(
  data_embeddings = review_embeddings,
  data_targets = review_labels,
  data_folds = 10,
  data_val_size = 0.25,
  loss_balance_class_weights = TRUE,
  loss_balance_sequence_length = TRUE,
  loss_cls_fct_name = "AEMLoss",
  #loss_cls_fct_name = "FocalLoss",
  use_sc = TRUE,
  sc_method = "knnor",
  sc_min_k = 1,
  sc_max_k = 10,
  use_pl = FALSE,
  pl_max_steps = 3,
  pl_max = 1.00,
  pl_anchor = 1.00,
  pl_min = 0.00,
  sustain_track = TRUE,
  sustain_iso_code = "DEU",
  sustain_region = NULL,
  sustain_interval = 15,
  sustain_log_level = "error",
  epochs = 2000,
  batch_size = 128,
  trace = TRUE,
  ml_trace = 1,
  log_dir = NULL,
  log_write_interval = 10,
  n_cores = auto_n_cores(),
  lr_rate = 0.0,
  lr_min = 0.0,
  lr_epochs = 30,
  lr_scheduler = "Linear",
  lr_warm_up_ratio = 0.10,
  optimizer = "AdamW",
  amp = TRUE,
  comp_use=TRUE,
  comp_mode="reduce-overhead"
)
```

First, we can analyse the training history of the performance estimation stage.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval = TRUE, fig.cap = paste0("Figure ",running_num_figures,": Training History of a Classifier with Feature Extractor during Performance Estimation Stage (loss)"),fig.align="center"}

## 7.5. Saving and Loading

If you would like to save and load a `TEFeatureExtractor` independently of a classifier, you can use the `save_to_disk` and `load_from_disk` functions, as with the other objects of this package. This is useful if you want to use the `TEFeatureExtractor` at a later point in time in combination with other models.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval=TRUE}
save_to_disk(
  object = feature_extractor,
  dir_path = "examples",
  folder_name = "feature_extractor"
)
```

# 8 Plots for Training History

## 8.1 BaseModels

You can use `BaseModels`, `TEFeatureExtractors` and classifiers to create plots showing your model's training process. The process of requesting these plots is similar for all objects. 
However, classifiers offer the greatest degree of customisation of graphics. 
This chapter demonstrates how to use the plots. We refer to models from previous chapters to provide examples.

We start with the base models. The `x_min`, `x_max`, `y_min` and `y_max` arguments allow you to zoom in or out. If you set these arguments to `NULL`, the values will be determined automatically.

The `ind_best_model` argument allows you to emphasise the epoch with the lowest loss for the validation sample. In general, this is the state of the model with the best generalisation abilities. Unlike the classifiers, this is also the final state of the model after training.
The `text_size` argument allows you to increase or decrease the size of the text within the graphic.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval=TRUE, fig.cap=paste0("Figure ",running_num_figures,": Example of a Training History for a BaseModel emphasizing the Best Model State.")}
base_model_bert$plot_training_history(
  x_min = NULL,
  x_max = NULL,
  y_min = NULL,
  y_max = NULL,
  ind_best_model = TRUE,
  text_size = 10L
)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
running_num_figures <- running_num_figures + 1
```

## 8.2 Classifiers

Classifiers offer a greater variety of options. Using the `x_min`, `x_max`, `y_min` and `y_max` arguments, you can specify the area to be plotted. Setting these arguments to `NULL` will generate adequate values automatically. With the `measure` argument, you can select the metric you would like to see.
For example, the following plot shows loss.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval=TRUE, fig.cap=paste0("Figure ",running_num_figures,": Example of a Training History for a Classifier emphasizing the Loss.")}
classifier$plot_training_history(
  final_training = FALSE,
  pl_step = NULL,
  measure = "loss",
  ind_best_model = FALSE,
  ind_selected_model = FALSE,
  x_min = NULL,
  x_max = NULL,
  y_min = NULL,
  y_max = NULL,
  add_min_max = FALSE,
  text_size = 10L
)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
running_num_figures <- running_num_figures + 1
```

The following plot shows how the average iota values changed over the course of the training process.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval=TRUE, fig.cap=paste0("Figure ",running_num_figures,": Example of a Training History for a Classifier emphasizing the Average Iota.")}
classifier$plot_training_history(
  final_training = FALSE,
  pl_step = NULL,
  measure = "avg_iota",
  ind_best_model = FALSE,
  ind_selected_model = FALSE,
  x_min = NULL,
  x_max = NULL,
  y_min = NULL,
  y_max = NULL,
  add_min_max = FALSE,
  text_size = 10L
)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
running_num_figures <- running_num_figures + 1
```

Setting `ind_best_model` to `TRUE` will display additional points in the graphic.
These points represents the epochs and their corresponding values according to the chosen metric 
at which the model performed best. For metrics such as loss, the values should be close to 0, 
while for metrics such as accuracy, balanced accuracy and average iota, the best 
values are close to 1. You can see one point for every fold during training.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval=TRUE, fig.cap=paste0("Figure ",running_num_figures,": Example of a Training History for a Classifier emphasizing the Loss and the best Model States.")}
classifier$plot_training_history(
  final_training = FALSE,
  pl_step = NULL,
  measure = "loss",
  ind_best_model = TRUE,
  ind_selected_model = FALSE,
  x_min = NULL,
  x_max = NULL,
  y_min = NULL,
  y_max = NULL,
  add_min_max = FALSE,
  text_size = 10L
)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
running_num_figures <- running_num_figures + 1
```

```{r, include = TRUE, eval=TRUE, fig.cap=paste0("Figure ",running_num_figures,": Example of a Training History for a Classifier emphasizing the Average Iota and the best Model States.")}
classifier$plot_training_history(
  final_training = FALSE,
  pl_step = NULL,
  measure = "avg_iota",
  ind_best_model = TRUE,
  ind_selected_model = FALSE,
  x_min = NULL,
  x_max = NULL,
  y_min = NULL,
  y_max = NULL,
  add_min_max = FALSE,
  text_size = 10L
)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
running_num_figures <- running_num_figures + 1
```

Please note that these points indicate the model's optimal state according to the chosen metric for each fold.
However, these values do not necessarily reflect the final state of the model. 
This is because the best state of a model during each training loop is determined by the best smoothed average iota value. If there are multiple models with the same smoothed average iota value, the model with the best loss is taken into account. Finally, the state with the highest number of epochs is used.

Set `ind_selected_model` to `TRUE` to add the final states of the model for every fold.

```{r, include = TRUE, eval=TRUE, fig.cap=paste0("Figure ",running_num_figures,": Example of a Training History for a Classifier emphasizing the Loss, the best Model States, and the Final Model States.")}
classifier$plot_training_history(
  final_training = FALSE,
  pl_step = NULL,
  measure = "loss",
  ind_best_model = TRUE,
  ind_selected_model = TRUE,
  x_min = NULL,
  x_max = NULL,
  y_min = NULL,
  y_max = NULL,
  add_min_max = FALSE,
  text_size = 10L
)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
running_num_figures <- running_num_figures + 1
```

Since the performance of a model is determined by several factors, the minimum and 
maximum values provide a deeper understanding of the training process. 
To include these in the plot, set `add_min_max` to `TRUE`. 
The plot will now show the full range of values for each epoch according to the chosen metric. 

```{r, include = TRUE, eval=TRUE, fig.cap=paste0("Figure ",running_num_figures,": Example of a Training History for a Classifier emphasizing the Loss with Minimal and Maximal Values.")}
classifier$plot_training_history(
  final_training = FALSE,
  pl_step = NULL,
  measure = "loss",
  ind_best_model = TRUE,
  ind_selected_model = TRUE,
  x_min = NULL,
  x_max = NULL,
  y_min = NULL,
  y_max = NULL,
  add_min_max = TRUE,
  text_size = 10L
)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
running_num_figures <- running_num_figures + 1
```

Using the argument `final_training`, you can switch between the performance estimation 
stage and the final training stage of the model. Since the final training phase 
only differentiates between training and validation data sets, there is no line 
for test data. In addition, there are no folds. Therefore, the argument `add_min_max` has no functionality. 

```{r, include = TRUE, eval=TRUE, fig.cap=paste0("Figure ",running_num_figures,": Example of a Training History for a Classifier emphasizing the Loss at the Final Training Phase.")}
classifier$plot_training_history(
  final_training = TRUE,
  pl_step = NULL,
  measure = "loss",
  ind_best_model = TRUE,
  ind_selected_model = TRUE,
  x_min = NULL,
  x_max = NULL,
  y_min = NULL,
  y_max = NULL,
  add_min_max = TRUE,
  text_size = 10L
)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
running_num_figures <- running_num_figures + 1
```

The final important argument is `pl_step`. 
This value is only relevant if the model used pseudo labeling during training. 
This parameter allows you to select the step during pseudo labeling 
that should be displayed in the plot. This works for performance estimation as well as the final training stage.
